'''Ngarluma''' and '''Kariyarra''' are members of a [[dialect continuum]], which is a part of the [[Ngayarda languages|Ngayarda language]] group of [[Western Australia]], in the [[Pama–Nyungan languages|Pama–Nyungan language family]]. Some sources suggest that an [[extinct language|extinct dialect]], '''[[Jaburara]]''', was a third member of the continuum.<ref>See, for example: {{cite book |first1=Lynette F. |last1=Oates |first2=William J. |last2=Oates |year=1970 |title=Aboriginal Languages of Australia: A Revised Linguistic Survey of Australia |location=Canberra |publisher=Australian Institute of Aboriginal Studies |isbn=0855750103 |id={{NLA|2163908}}}}</ref> However, it is clear that Jaburara had a distinct identity that has been partly obscured by a [[Flying Foam Massacre|collapse in the numbers of Jaburara speakers]] during the late 19th century, and there is some evidence that Jaburara may have instead been a dialect of [[Martuthunira language|Martuthunira]] (see below).

While Ngarluma and Kariyarra, as parts of a continuum, are [[mutually intelligible]], they are considered distinct languages by their speakers, reflecting an ethnic division between the [[Ngarluma people|Ngarluma]] and [[Kariyarra people]]s. As such they may be regarded as a single, [[pluricentric language]].

Under [[Carl Georg von Brandenstein]]'s 1967 classification scheme, Ngarluma was classed as a "Coastal Ngayarda" (or Ngaryarta) language, but the separation of the group into "Coastal" and "Inland" groups is no longer considered valid.

Apart from the division between Ngarluma and Kariyarra, there are either three or four sub-dialects within Ngarluma. However, the inclusion of Jaburara – which parallels a belief amongst Ngarluma people that the [[Yapurarra|Jaburara people]] and their traditional land were a sub-group of the Ngarluma people and lands – is controversial. There are two reasons for this: the Jaburara dialect is sometimes considered a dialect in its own right, or a dialect of Martuthunira. There is evidence for the latter theory in the word ''jaburara'', which means "northerners" in the languages of the region:<ref>{{cite web |url=http://coombs.anu.edu.au/WWWVLPages/AborigPages/LANG/WA/4_4.htm |first=Nicholas |last=Thieberger |year=1996 |title=4.4 North of the Gascoyne River to Port Hedland |website=Handbook of Western Australian Aboriginal languages south of the Kimberley |access-date=12 October 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/19970104041357/http://coombs.anu.edu.au/WWWVLPages/AborigPages/LANG/WA/4_4.htm |archive-date=1997-01-04}}</ref> the traditional lands of the Jaburara, on and around the [[Burrup Peninsula]], are generally to the north of the [[Martuthunira people|Martuthunira]] lands (whereas the Jaburara are mostly west of the Ngarluma lands).

A [[pidgin]]ized form of Ngarluma was once used as a contact language in the area.<ref>{{cite journal |first=Alan |last=Dench |year=1998 |title=Pidgin Ngarluma: an indigenous contact language in North Western Australia |journal=Journal of Pidgin and Creole Languages |volume=13 |issue=1 |pages=1–20|doi=10.1075/jpcl.13.1.02den }}</ref>

==Linguistic area/boundaries==
Kariyarra people, prior to European settlement occupied an area from the [[Yule River]] east to [[Port Hedland]] and south to the [[Hamersley Range]].

The official Ngarluma [[Native title in Australia#Native title determinations|Native Title Determination]] Area  (including the Jaburara lands) covers the area southward from [[Point Samson, Western Australia|Point Samson]], [[Cossack, Western Australia|Cossack]], [[Wickham, Western Australia|Wickham]], [[Roebourne, Western Australia|Roebourne]], to the northern boundary of [[Millstream-Chichester National Park]] and; from the east side of the mouth of the [[Maitland River (Western Australia)|Maitland River]] to the west side of the [[Peawah River]] near [[Whim Creek]], including the towns of [[Dampier, Western Australia|Dampier]] and [[Karratha, Western Australia|Karratha]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.ngarluma.com.au/ |title=Ngarluma Aboriginal Corporation |year=2012 |publisher=Ngarluma Aboriginal Corporation |access-date=12 October 2012}}</ref>

However, this boundary is controversial for two reasons: it includes areas also regarded as traditional country by many Martuthunira people and; for legal reasons, it does not include areas that many Ngarluma people consider to fall into their traditional country.{{citation needed|date=July 2024}}
